questions.topic: Introduction to TensorFlow: strengths, challenges, new features
questions.ideal_answer: TensorFlow is an open-source machine learning and deep learning framework developed by Google. It represents computations on multi-dimensional arrays called tensors and can run them on CPUs, GPUs and TPUs. It provides the high-level Keras API for building and training neural networks easily. It also supports deployment to servers, mobile devices through TensorFlow Lite and browsers through TensorFlow.js.

questions.topic: Computation graphs, tensors, variables, placeholders and constants
questions.text: What is a tensor in TensorFlow?
questions.ideal_answer: A tensor is a multi-dimensional array of values with a uniform data type, and it is the basic data structure in TensorFlow. A scalar is a rank-0 tensor, a vector is rank 1, a matrix is rank 2, and higher dimensions give rank-3 or more tensors. Each tensor has a shape, which gives the size of each dimension, and a dtype such as float32. Tensors flow between operations in a computation graph, which gives TensorFlow its name.

questions.topic: Computation graphs, tensors, variables, placeholders and constants
questions.text: What is the difference between a tf.constant and a tf.Variable?
questions.ideal_answer: A tf.constant is an immutable tensor whose value cannot be changed after it is created. A tf.Variable holds a value that can be modified during execution, using methods like assign. Variables are used to store model parameters such as weights and biases, which are updated during training by the optimizer. Constants are used for fixed values like hyperparameters or input data that do not change.

questions.text: What is the difference between overfitting and underfitting?
questions.ideal_answer: Overfitting happens when a model learns the training data too well, including noise, so it has high training accuracy but performs poorly on new or validation data. Underfitting happens when a model is too simple to capture the underlying pattern, so it performs poorly on both training and validation data. Overfitting is linked to high variance and underfitting to high bias. They are detected by comparing training and validation loss curves.

questions.topic: Image classification with Fashion MNIST using Keras
questions.text: Describe the steps to build an image classifier for Fashion MNIST using Keras.
questions.ideal_answer: First load the Fashion MNIST dataset, which has 60,000 training and 10,000 test grayscale images of size 28 by 28 in 10 clothing classes, and scale pixel values to the range 0 to 1. Build a Sequential model with a Flatten layer to convert each image into 784 values, a Dense hidden layer with ReLU activation, and a Dense output layer with 10 units and softmax. Compile it with the Adam optimizer, sparse categorical cross-entropy loss and accuracy metric. Then train it with model.fit for some epochs and evaluate on the test set with model.evaluate.

questions.topic: Building and training neural networks with gradient descent
questions.text: How does gradient descent train a neural network?
questions.ideal_answer: Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm that minimizes the loss function by adjusting the weights. In each step the network does a forward pass to compute predictions and loss, then backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. Each weight is updated by moving in the opposite direction of the gradient: new weight = old weight minus learning rate times gradient. This repeats over many batches and epochs until the loss converges, and variants include stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent and Adam.

questions.topic: Regression with linear models and deep neural networks
questions.text: For a regression problem in Keras, why do we use a linear output and mean squared error rather than softmax and cross-entropy?
questions.ideal_answer: In regression the target is a continuous number, such as a house price, so the output layer has a single unit with no activation, meaning a linear output that can take any real value. Softmax outputs probabilities across classes that add up to 1, which only makes sense for classification. Mean squared error, or mean absolute error, measures how far the predicted numbers are from the true numbers. Cross-entropy measures differences between probability distributions, so it is not suitable for continuous targets.

questions.topic: Convolutional neural networks on MNIST and CIFAR-10
questions.text: Why are convolutional neural networks better than fully connected networks for image classification on datasets like CIFAR-10?
questions.ideal_answer: Convolutional layers use small filters that slide across the image, so they detect local patterns such as edges and textures and share the same weights at every position. Weight sharing greatly reduces the number of parameters compared with a dense layer connected to every pixel, which reduces overfitting and computation. Pooling layers reduce spatial size and give some translation invariance. CNNs also preserve the 2D spatial structure that flattening destroys, and they build hierarchical features from edges to shapes to objects.

questions.text: Your Keras model reaches 99% training accuracy but only 70% validation accuracy. How would you fix this?
questions.ideal_answer: This is overfitting, because the model memorises the training data and does not generalise. Remedies include adding dropout layers, L1 or L2 weight regularization, and reducing model complexity by using fewer layers or units. Getting more data or using data augmentation, such as flips and rotations for images, also helps. Early stopping with a callback that monitors validation loss stops training before overfitting gets worse, and batch normalization can also help.

questions.topic: RNNs and LSTM for text generation and sentiment analysis
questions.text: Why do simple RNNs struggle with long sentences, and how does an LSTM solve this?
questions.ideal_answer: Simple RNNs are trained with backpropagation through time, and over many time steps the gradients get multiplied repeatedly, so they shrink towards zero, which is the vanishing gradient problem. As a result they forget information from early in a long sequence. An LSTM adds a cell state and three gates: the forget gate, input gate and output gate. These gates control what information to keep, add or output, letting gradients flow across many steps and capture long-term dependencies.

questions.topic: Text classification and sentiment analysis on IMDB; TensorFlow Hub
questions.text: You must build a sentiment classifier for product reviews quickly with limited labelled data. How would you use TensorFlow Hub and what trade-offs would you consider?
questions.ideal_answer: I would use transfer learning by loading a pre-trained text embedding or model from TensorFlow Hub as a KerasLayer and adding a small dense classification head on top. Because the embedding already captures language meaning from a large corpus, the model needs far less labelled data and trains faster. I could first freeze the pre-trained layer and later fine-tune it with a low learning rate if more data is available. Trade-offs include model size and inference latency, whether the pre-trained domain matches product reviews, licence terms, and the risk of overfitting when fine-tuning on little data.

questions.topic: Installing TensorFlow, Keras, Jupyter and Matplotlib
questions.text: Your team members get different results and import errors when running the same TensorFlow notebook. How would you set up a reliable development environment?
questions.ideal_answer: Each project should use an isolated virtual environment, such as venv or conda, so packages do not conflict with the system Python. Pin exact versions of TensorFlow, Keras, NumPy, Matplotlib and Jupyter in a requirements.txt or environment file so everyone installs the same versions. GPU users must match TensorFlow with compatible CUDA and cuDNN versions, or a Docker image can be used for full reproducibility. To get consistent results, also set random seeds and record the dataset version.
